title: Idioms, slang and regional speech
objectives: I can understand common Brazilian slang, fillers and idioms in relaxed conversation.
I can recognize regional words and accents from the Southeast, Minas Gerais, the Northeast and the South.
I can use discourse markers such as tipo, né, aí and sei lá to sound natural in informal speech.
I can tell slang apart from vulgar language and from formal register, and choose the right one for the situation.

vocabulary.note: Also means 'type' or 'kind' as a noun. As a filler it introduces an example or softens a statement.

example.pt: Tipo, eu nem sabia que ele ia viajar.
example.en: Like, I did not even know he was going to travel.

vocabulary.note: Contraction of não é. Used as a tag question at the end of a sentence or as a filler.

example.pt: Tá frio hoje, né?
example.en: It is cold today, isn't it?

vocabulary.note: Mild exclamation of surprise or complaint, very common in Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo.

example.pt: Pô, você podia ter avisado!
example.en: Man, you could have let me know!

vocabulary.note: Used to address a friend of any gender, or to say 'guy'. Feminine a cara means 'the face'.

example.pt: Cara, você viu o jogo ontem?
example.en: Dude, did you see the game yesterday?

vocabulary.note: Typical of São Paulo. In Rio the equivalent is mermão.

example.pt: Mano, esse filme é muito bom.
example.en: Bro, this movie is really good.

vocabulary.note: Casual way to express uncertainty or indifference.

example.pt: Sei lá, acho que ele esqueceu.
example.en: I don't know, I think he forgot.

vocabulary.en: yeah, that's how it is, well
vocabulary.note: Agrees with what was said, often with a tone of resignation. Also used to open an explanation.

example.pt: Pois é, a reunião foi cancelada de novo.
example.en: Yeah, the meeting was cancelled again.

vocabulary.en: to find a way, to sort it out

example.pt: Vou dar um jeito de chegar a tempo.
example.en: I will find a way to arrive on time.

example.pt: Fica de olho na panela, por favor.
example.en: Keep an eye on the pot, please.

vocabulary.en: to take the blame, to get stuck with the consequences
vocabulary.note: Literally 'to pay the duck'. Used when someone suffers for a mistake that was not theirs.

example.pt: Eu não fiz nada e acabei pagando o pato.
example.en: I did nothing and ended up taking the blame.

vocabulary.en: to have one's head in the clouds
vocabulary.note: Can mean distracted or very happy, depending on the context.

example.pt: Ela está nas nuvens desde que ganhou o prêmio.
example.en: She has been over the moon since she won the prize.

vocabulary.en: to stay relaxed, to be fine with it

example.pt: Pode ficar de boa, eu resolvo isso.
example.en: You can relax, I will handle it.

vocabulary.en: to pay attention to, to take seriously
vocabulary.note: Often used in the negative. Dar bola para alguém can also mean to show romantic interest.

example.pt: Não dê bola para o que ele diz.
example.en: Don't pay attention to what he says.

vocabulary.note: From old public telephones that needed a token (ficha) to work.

example.pt: Só agora caiu a ficha de que eu me formei.
example.en: Only now has it sunk in that I graduated.

vocabulary.en: to cost an arm and a leg

example.pt: Esse celular custou os olhos da cara.
example.en: This phone cost an arm and a leg.

vocabulary.en: to swallow one's pride, to put up with something unpleasant

example.pt: Tive que engolir sapo no trabalho hoje.
example.en: I had to swallow my pride at work today.

vocabulary.pt: ficar com a pulga atrás da orelha

example.pt: Fiquei com a pulga atrás da orelha quando ele mudou de assunto.
example.en: I became suspicious when he changed the subject.

example.pt: Meu tio é mão de vaca, nunca paga a conta.
example.en: My uncle is stingy, he never pays the bill.

vocabulary.en: to deal with a tough problem
vocabulary.note: Literally 'to peel a pineapple'. An abacaxi is also a difficult problem.

example.pt: Hoje a equipe vai ter que descascar um abacaxi.
example.en: Today the team will have to tackle a tough problem.

vocabulary.note: The same root vegetable is called mandioca in São Paulo and much of the country, and aipim in Rio and the South.

example.pt: No café da manhã, ela comeu macaxeira com manteiga.
example.en: For breakfast she ate cassava with butter.

vocabulary.note: Called mexerica in São Paulo and Minas Gerais, and tangerina in much of the rest of the country.

example.pt: Os gaúchos comem bergamota no inverno.
example.en: People from Rio Grande do Sul eat tangerines in winter.

vocabulary.note: Marks surprise or obviousness; the signature interjection of Minas Gerais.

example.pt: Uai, você não sabia que o ônibus já saiu?
example.en: Well, didn't you know the bus already left?

vocabulary.note: Expresses surprise, fear or admiration. Oxente is a related Northeastern interjection.

example.pt: Eita, que confusão é essa aqui?
example.en: Whoa, what is this mess here?

vocabulary.note: Gaúcho interjection, often paired with tchê, a friendly form of address.

example.pt: Bah, que frio hoje, tchê!
example.en: Wow, it is cold today, mate!

vocabulary.note: Mild exclamation of annoyance or surprise, common in São Paulo. Avoid it in formal settings.

example.pt: Putz, esqueci a chave em casa.
example.en: Oops, I left the key at home.

dialogues.title: Comemorando uma vaga nova
dialogues.context: Three friends in São Paulo talk at a bar after work. Their speech is relaxed and full of fillers.

lines.speaker: Rafa
lines.pt: Cara, você viu o jogo ontem? Foi, tipo, a melhor partida do ano.
lines.en: Dude, did you see the game yesterday? It was, like, the best match of the year.

lines.speaker: Léo
lines.pt: Não vi, mano. Fiquei preso no trabalho até tarde.
lines.en: I didn't, bro. I was stuck at work until late.

lines.speaker: Bia
lines.pt: Pô, Léo, de novo? Cê tá trabalhando demais, né?
lines.en: Man, Léo, again? You are working too much, aren't you?

lines.speaker: Léo
lines.pt: Pois é. Sei lá, acho que meu chefe tá me testando.
lines.en: Yeah. I don't know, I think my boss is testing me.

lines.speaker: Rafa
lines.pt: Fica de boa, cara. Você sempre dá um jeito.
lines.en: Take it easy, man. You always find a way.

lines.speaker: Bia
lines.pt: Eu também tô meio nas nuvens hoje. Ontem me ofereceram uma vaga nova e ainda não caiu a ficha.
lines.en: I am a bit in the clouds today too. Yesterday they offered me a new position and it still hasn't sunk in.

lines.speaker: Léo
lines.pt: Nossa, Bia, parabéns! Então vamo comemorar hoje à noite!
lines.en: Wow, Bia, congratulations! Then let's celebrate tonight!

lines.speaker: Rafa
lines.pt: Aí sim! Eu conheço uma pizzaria boa e barata aqui perto.
lines.en: Now you're talking! I know a good, cheap pizzeria near here.

lines.speaker: Bia
lines.pt: Tá bom, mas dessa vez a conta é dividida, né?
lines.en: Okay, but this time we split the bill, right?

lines.speaker: Léo
lines.pt: Claro. Mas, sei lá, se o Rafa pedir o cardápio inteiro, eu não pago.
lines.en: Of course. But, I don't know, if Rafa orders the whole menu, I'm not paying.

dialogues.title: Cada canto com seu nome
dialogues.context: Three colleagues from different regions have lunch at a farm in Minas Gerais and compare what they call the same foods.

lines.speaker: Zé
lines.pt: Uai, Marina, vai querer mais um pouco de mandioca frita?
lines.en: Well, Marina, do you want a bit more fried cassava?

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.pt: Nossa, que delícia! Lá no Rio a gente fala aipim, mas é a mesma coisa, né?
lines.en: Wow, how delicious! In Rio we say aipim, but it is the same thing, right?

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.pt: No Sul também é aipim. E a Tati, lá do Recife, chama de macaxeira.
lines.en: In the South it is aipim too. And Tati, from Recife, calls it macaxeira.

lines.speaker: Zé
lines.pt: Uai, cada canto do Brasil tem um nome pra tudo, sô!
lines.en: Well, every corner of Brazil has its own name for everything!

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.pt: Verdade. Outro dia, no mercado, pedi mexerica e a moça não entendeu nada.
lines.en: True. The other day at the market I asked for mexerica and the woman had no idea what I meant.

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.pt: Bah, lá no Sul a gente fala bergamota. Ninguém diz mexerica.
lines.en: Wow, down South we say bergamota. Nobody says mexerica.

lines.speaker: Zé
lines.pt: Em Minas é mexerica, mas tem gente que fala tangerina também.
lines.en: In Minas it is mexerica, but some people say tangerina too.

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.pt: Lúcia, lá em Porto Alegre vocês falam tu, não é?
lines.en: Lúcia, in Porto Alegre you say tu, don't you?

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.pt: Falamos, sim! Lá é tu vai, tu quer, bem solto. Em casa eu ainda falo tchê com os guris.
lines.en: We do! There it is tu vai, tu quer, very loose. At home I still say tchê to the kids.

lines.speaker: Zé
lines.pt: Minha avó chamava tudo de trem: passa o trem pra cá, pega aquele trem ali.
lines.en: My grandmother called everything trem: pass the thing over here, grab that thing over there.

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.pt: Adorei! Agora entendo por que o sotaque de vocês é tão musical.
lines.en: I loved it! Now I understand why your accents are so musical.

dialogues.title: Depois da apresentação
dialogues.context: A presentation went badly at an advertising agency. Three colleagues talk it over using office idioms.

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.pt: Pedro, deu tudo errado na apresentação. O cliente ficou com a pulga atrás da orelha.
lines.en: Pedro, everything went wrong in the presentation. The client became suspicious.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: Eu sei. E o pior é que eu não fiz nada e acabei pagando o pato.
lines.en: I know. And the worst part is that I did nothing and ended up taking the blame.

lines.speaker: Vera
lines.pt: Calma, gente. Vamos dar um jeito. Quem ficou de olho nos números?
lines.en: Calm down, everyone. We will find a way. Who kept an eye on the numbers?

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.pt: Fui eu, mas os dados chegaram errados. Tive que engolir sapo quando o diretor reclamou.
lines.en: It was me, but the data arrived wrong. I had to swallow my pride when the director complained.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: O programa novo custou os olhos da cara e ainda não funciona direito.
lines.en: The new software cost an arm and a leg and still doesn't work properly.

lines.speaker: Vera
lines.pt: Pois é. E o diretor anda nas nuvens, não dá bola para nenhum relatório.
lines.en: Yes. And the director is in the clouds, he doesn't pay attention to any report.

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.pt: Só agora caiu a ficha de que precisamos refazer tudo até sexta.
lines.en: Only now has it sunk in that we need to redo everything by Friday.

lines.speaker: Vera
lines.pt: Então mãos à obra. Pedro, você refaz os gráficos, e a Camila fala com o cliente.
lines.en: Then let's get to work. Pedro, you redo the charts, and Camila talks to the client.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: Fechado. Mas amanhã eu pago o café, que hoje a coisa tá feia.
lines.en: Deal. But tomorrow I'm buying the coffee, because today things look bad.

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.pt: Combinado. Bora trabalhar, que esse abacaxi não vai se descascar sozinho.
lines.en: Agreed. Let's get to work, because this problem won't solve itself.

grammar.title: Discourse markers in everyday speech
grammar.explanation:
Discourse markers are the small words that organize spoken Brazilian Portuguese: they open an idea, soften a statement, ask for agreement or signal a change of topic. They carry little literal meaning, so dictionary translations rarely help; what matters is the function.

Tipo introduces an example or hedges ('like'). Né asks for confirmation and is short for não é. Aí ('then, so') moves a story forward and is the everyday replacement for então or depois in narration. Então restarts or wraps up a point. Pô, cara and mano are vocatives and interjections that show familiarity. Pois é agrees or concedes. Sei lá expresses doubt or indifference. É isso closes a thought: 'that's it'. Tá and tá bom mean 'okay'.

In writing, in interviews and in meetings with people you do not know, use them very sparingly. Overusing tipo and né sounds careless in formal contexts, but using none at all sounds stiff among friends.

examples.pt: Aí eu cheguei lá, né, e a loja já tinha fechado.
examples.en: So I got there, right, and the store had already closed.

examples.pt: Tipo, eu gosto dele, mas não sei se quero namorar.
examples.en: Like, I like him, but I don't know if I want to date.

examples.pt: Então, é isso: a gente se vê amanhã.
examples.en: So, that's it: we will see each other tomorrow.

examples.pt: Pois é, eu também achei estranho.
examples.en: Yeah, I thought it was strange too.

examples.pt: Sei lá, cara, depende do dia.
examples.en: I don't know, man, it depends on the day.

grammar.title: Regional variation: vocabulary, accents and tu versus você
grammar.explanation:
Brazilian Portuguese is remarkably uniform in writing, but speech and everyday vocabulary change from region to region. Brazilians usually recognize each other's origin within a sentence or two.

The carioca accent (Rio) pronounces final s and preconsonantal s as sh and uses pô and mermão. The paulistano accent is flatter, with mano and meu. In Minas Gerais speakers swallow syllables, say uai and sô, and use trem for 'thing'. In the Northeast vowels are open and musical; eita, oxente and visse are typical. In the South, especially Rio Grande do Sul, bah and tchê are frequent and guri or guria means boy or girl.

For 'you', most of Brazil uses você with third person verbs. Tu is normal in parts of the North, the Northeast, Rio Grande do Sul and Florianópolis, and in many places it is combined with the third person verb (tu vai, tu quer). Correct tu forms (tu vais, tu queres) are less common in speech and are more a mark of writing or of certain areas. As a learner, você is always safe.

rows: Pernambuco and much of the Northeast

examples.pt: No Nordeste, a mandioca também se chama macaxeira.
examples.en: In the Northeast, mandioca is also called macaxeira.

examples.pt: Lá em Porto Alegre, muita gente fala tu vai em vez de você vai.
examples.en: In Porto Alegre, many people say tu vai instead of você vai.

examples.pt: Em Minas, o pessoal diz uai quando fica surpreso.
examples.en: In Minas, people say uai when they are surprised.

examples.pt: O carioca fala mermão, e o paulistano fala mano.
examples.en: The person from Rio says mermão, and the person from São Paulo says mano.

examples.pt: Na padaria, pedi mexerica e a atendente gaúcha pediu para eu repetir.
examples.en: At the bakery I asked for mexerica and the attendant from the South asked me to repeat it.

grammar.title: Idioms with animals, food and body parts
grammar.explanation:
Portuguese idioms are fixed phrases whose meaning cannot be guessed from the words. Many use everyday images: animals (pagar o pato, pulga atrás da orelha, mão de vaca), food (descascar um abacaxi, engolir sapo) and body parts (custar os olhos da cara, ficar de olho). Learn each one as a block and keep its verb forms flexible: ficar de olho becomes fica de olho, ficou de olho, ficando de olho.

Some idioms combine with the verb ficar or dar, which are extremely productive in Brazilian Portuguese: ficar de boa, ficar na dúvida, dar um jeito, dar bola, dar uma força. In the negative, dar bola usually means ignoring someone or something: não dê bola.

Many idioms are informal, but they are not vulgar. They can be used in a relaxed conversation with colleagues, yet in formal writing it is better to use a plain equivalent, such as prestar atenção instead of dar bola, or ser avarento instead of ser mão de vaca.

rows: cost the eyes of the face

examples.pt: Ninguém quer descascar esse abacaxi sozinho.
examples.en: Nobody wants to tackle this tough problem alone.

examples.pt: Ela ficou de olho no relógio a reunião inteira.
examples.en: She kept an eye on the clock the whole meeting.

examples.pt: Quando vi o preço, quase caí para trás: custou os olhos da cara.
examples.en: When I saw the price I nearly fell over: it cost an arm and a leg.

examples.pt: Ele vive engolindo sapo para não brigar com o chefe.
examples.en: He is always swallowing his pride so as not to fight with his boss.

examples.pt: Não dê bola para o que os outros falam.
examples.en: Don't pay attention to what others say.

grammar.title: Register: slang, vulgarity and informal contractions
grammar.explanation:
Brazilian Portuguese has three distinct layers. Gíria (slang) is informal but harmless: tipo, mano, de boa, bora. Palavrão (vulgar language) is offensive and should be avoided by learners until the context is completely clear. Formal register is used for writing, work and official situations. Choosing the right one matters more than knowing the word.

In speech, several contractions are completely standard among native speakers: está becomes tá, estou becomes tô, para becomes pra, você becomes cê, não becomes num (or nã), vamos becomes vamo, and não é becomes né. They are not errors, but they are not written in formal texts either. Note that pra and tá appear often in informal writing, such as messages and social media, but never in a letter to a company.

A practical rule: match the register of the person you are talking to. When in doubt, use the plain full form. It is never rude to speak slightly more formally than needed, but slang in the wrong place can be awkward.

examples.pt: Cê tá indo pra onde, cara?
examples.en: Where are you going, man?

examples.pt: Eu num sei, tô meio cansado hoje.
examples.en: I don't know, I am a bit tired today.

examples.pt: Vamo lá, que a gente tá atrasado.
examples.en: Come on, because we are late.

examples.pt: Não sei ao certo; vou verificar e lhe informo.
examples.en: I am not sure; I will check and let you know.

examples.pt: Na entrevista, falei de forma simples e educada, sem gíria.
examples.en: In the interview I spoke simply and politely, without slang.

culture.title: O sotaque como identidade
culture.text:
In Brazil an accent, or sotaque, is a strong marker of identity, and it is also a source of humor and affection. People from Rio are known for the chiado, the sh sound at the end of syllables. Paulistanos are teased for saying meu and mano, and for the so-called R caipira of the countryside of São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Goiás. The Northeast is admired for its rhythm and its colorful interjections. Gaúchos are recognized by bah, tchê and their tu forms.

For decades, television newscasts tried to create a neutral accent, which is why national anchors sounded almost regionless. Today that is changing: streaming series, podcasts and social media give space to real local speech, and expressions such as uai, oxente and bah have spread across the country. Still, prejudice against some accents exists, especially toward the Northeast and the rural interior, and many people change their speech when they move to another city.

For a learner, the best approach is to listen widely and to be flexible. Brazilians generally appreciate any effort to speak their language, and asking 'Como vocês chamam isso aqui?' is a very good conversation starter. Be careful with slang that sounds too local or too crude: it is better to understand it than to imitate it right away.

paragraphs.pt: Quando Juliana saiu de Recife para morar em Porto Alegre, achou que a mudança seria apenas de cidade. Logo no primeiro dia, porém, percebeu que teria de aprender uma nova língua dentro da própria língua.
paragraphs.en: When Juliana left Recife to live in Porto Alegre, she thought the change would be only one of city. On the very first day, however, she realized she would have to learn a new language inside her own language.

paragraphs.pt: No mercado, pediu macaxeira e a atendente olhou para ela sem entender. Depois de rir um pouco, a moça explicou que ali se dizia aipim.
paragraphs.en: At the market she asked for macaxeira and the attendant looked at her without understanding. After laughing a little, the woman explained that there they said aipim.

paragraphs.pt: Nas semanas seguintes, as surpresas continuaram. Os colegas da faculdade diziam bah e tchê a cada frase, e a palavra guri aparecia o tempo todo para falar de menino.
paragraphs.en: In the following weeks, the surprises continued. Her college classmates said bah and tchê in every sentence, and the word guri appeared all the time to mean boy.

paragraphs.pt: Juliana, que sempre dizia oxente quando ficava espantada, descobriu que ninguém entendia a expressão. Por outro lado, todos adoravam o jeito cantado com que ela falava.
paragraphs.en: Juliana, who had always said oxente when she was astonished, discovered that nobody understood the expression. On the other hand, everybody loved the singsong way she spoke.

paragraphs.pt: Com o tempo, ela aprendeu a misturar os dois mundos. Hoje diz bergamota em vez de tangerina quando está no Sul, mas continua dizendo macaxeira quando liga para a mãe.
paragraphs.en: With time she learned to mix the two worlds. Today she says bergamota instead of tangerina when she is in the South, but she keeps saying macaxeira when she calls her mother.

paragraphs.pt: Quando volta a Recife, os amigos brincam que ela está falando gaúcho. Juliana responde que não há problema: um sotaque não se perde, só ganha mais camadas.
paragraphs.en: When she goes back to Recife, her friends joke that she is speaking gaúcho. Juliana answers that this is no problem: an accent is not lost, it just gains more layers.

questions.prompt: Why did the attendant not understand Juliana at the market?
choices: Juliana used the Northeastern word for a vegetable that is called aipim in Porto Alegre
The market did not sell that vegetable
questions.explanation: Macaxeira is the Northeastern name for what is called aipim in the South.

questions.prompt: What did Juliana discover about the expression oxente?
choices: Everybody used it in Porto Alegre
It is rude in the South
questions.explanation: The text says ninguém entendia a expressão.

questions.prompt: How do Juliana's friends in Recife react when she visits?
choices: They say she speaks like someone from Rio Grande do Sul
They ask her to teach them tchê
questions.explanation: They joke that she is falando gaúcho.

questions.prompt: What is Juliana's attitude at the end of the text?
choices: She wants to lose her accent
She believes an accent adds layers instead of being lost
She refuses to use Southern words
questions.explanation: Her conclusion is that um sotaque não se perde, só ganha mais camadas.

readings.title: Por que a gíria muda tão rápido?

paragraphs.pt: A gíria é a parte da língua que mais rapidamente se transforma.
paragraphs.en: Slang is the part of language that changes most quickly.

paragraphs.pt: Nos anos noventa, muita gente dizia que algo era maneiro ou irado; hoje, os jovens preferem expressões diferentes, e essas palavras já soam antigas para eles.
paragraphs.en: In the nineties many people said something was maneiro or irado; today young people prefer different expressions, and those words already sound old to them.

paragraphs.pt: Por isso, quem aprende português pela televisão ou por músicas antigas pode acabar falando como uma geração passada.
paragraphs.en: For this reason, someone who learns Portuguese from television or old songs may end up speaking like a past generation.

paragraphs.pt: Muitas gírias nascem em grupos específicos, como torcidas de futebol, comunidades do funk, surfistas e skatistas, e depois se espalham pelas redes sociais.
paragraphs.en: Many slang words are born in specific groups, such as soccer fan clubs, funk communities, surfers and skaters, and then spread through social media.

paragraphs.pt: Quando uma expressão chega à televisão e à publicidade, os jovens já estão procurando outra.
paragraphs.en: When an expression reaches television and advertising, young people are already looking for another one.

paragraphs.pt: Esse movimento constante explica por que falar como um adolescente costuma parecer forçado para quem já passou dessa idade.
paragraphs.en: This constant movement explains why talking like a teenager usually seems forced for someone who is past that age.

paragraphs.pt: Os linguistas lembram que gíria não é erro. É uma escolha de registro: entre amigos ela cria proximidade, mas em uma entrevista de emprego pode causar má impressão.
paragraphs.en: Linguists point out that slang is not a mistake. It is a choice of register: among friends it creates closeness, but in a job interview it can make a bad impression.

paragraphs.pt: Também é preciso distinguir a gíria do palavrão. A primeira é informal, porém em geral inofensiva; o segundo é ofensivo e deve ser evitado por estrangeiros até que conheçam bem o contexto.
paragraphs.en: It is also necessary to distinguish slang from swearing. The first is informal but generally harmless; the second is offensive and should be avoided by foreigners until they know the context well.

questions.prompt: According to the text, why can old songs be a risky way to learn slang?
choices: They have too many foreign words
They may teach expressions that sound old to a younger generation
They are always in a regional accent
questions.explanation: Slang changes quickly, so older material can sound dated.

questions.prompt: Where do many slang expressions originate?
choices: In specific groups such as fan clubs, surfers and skaters
questions.explanation: The text lists torcidas de futebol, comunidades do funk, surfistas e skatistas.

questions.prompt: What is the linguists' view of slang?
choices: It is a mistake that should be corrected
It is a choice of register that fits some situations and not others
It is only used by children
It is the same thing as swearing
questions.explanation: The text says gíria não é erro, é uma escolha de registro.

exercises.prompt: What does the expression cair a ficha mean?
choices: To finally realize or understand something
exercises.explanation: Literally 'for the token to drop'; it is used when something finally sinks in.

exercises.prompt: Which word do people in Recife use for mandioca?
exercises.explanation: Macaxeira is the Northeastern word; aipim is used in Rio and the South.

exercises.prompt: Eu não fiz nada e acabei pagando o pato. What happened?
choices: I was punished for something I did not do
exercises.explanation: Pagar o pato means to take the blame or suffer the consequences.

exercises.prompt: Which reply is best in a formal meeting with a client?
choices: Não tenho certeza, mas posso verificar e informar o senhor.

exercises.prompt: Which interjection is most typical of Minas Gerais?
exercises.explanation: Uai is the signature interjection of Minas; bah is gaúcho and eita is Northeastern.

exercises.prompt: Fica de olho na mala. What is the speaker asking?
choices: To keep watch over the suitcase
exercises.explanation: Ficar de olho means to keep an eye on something.

exercises.prompt_pt: Esse carro custou os ___ da cara.

exercises.hint_en: It is cold today, isn't it?

exercises.prompt_pt: Não se preocupe, eu vou dar um ___.

exercises.prompt_pt: Só agora ___ a ficha de que ele foi embora.
exercises.hint_en: Only now has it sunk in that he left.
exercises.explanation: Cair a ficha is used in the preterite when the realization has just happened.

exercises.prompt_pt: Eu não fiz nada e acabei ___ o pato.
